title: What is known about 1RB1RD_1RC1RB_1LD0RA_1RA0LE_1LF0LC_---1LE
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1RD_1RC1RB_1LD0RA_1RA0LE_1LF0LC_---1LE.
intro: This six-state, two-symbol Turing machine was one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. It halts: Lean and Coq each prove it, with a simulator that is proved correct and then evaluated from blank tape to the halting transition. The Coq proof also proves the exact number of steps. This page lists what has been established, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: It halts. Proved in Lean (halts, lean/Halt.lean): a run-length simulator with closed-form jumps is proved to follow the machine (kernel), and its run from blank tape reaches the halting transition (native_decide, which trusts Lean's compiler). It is also proved in Coq on busycoq's definitions (halts_172044, steps_172044, coq/). There the evaluation is done by the kernel's virtual machine, so that proof does not trust a compiler, and it counts every step. The number of steps, 853177647932005270554892218084645935472995035642746848454477793277027802995098762076895667304703808111420498351739937140047615589683 (about 8.53·10131), is proved in Coq: the machine reaches its halting configuration after exactly that number minus one steps and at no other time (kernel). Three separately written simulators agree with it. The tape is a binary odometer whose digits are counters of the word 011; each counter is a fuel tank that loses a unit every 2j visits of the right end. After 9.6·1065 visits the odometer is the whole tape, 2.9·1066 cells, every bit is 1, and the carry falls off the left end.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: The machine halts: a second proof, in Coq (busycoq)
claims.text: halts_172044 : halts tm c0 on the definitions of busycoq's BB6 branch, with no axioms. The same method as the Lean proof (the visit rule and the closed-form jump, proved for every zone; a run-length simulator proved to follow the machine) plus two block rules that cross a whole counter level in one round (D leftwards over 1 0 (011)k 1, C rightwards over (100)m 1 0 1 1 0, proved for every k, m). They bring the run from 88.9 to 19.0 million rounds. The run from blank tape to F0 is evaluated by vm_compute, which the kernel checks: about 8.5 minutes with the step counts below (160 seconds without them, in an earlier version on the busycoq fork).

claims.title: The exact number of steps: 8.53·10<sup>131</sup>
claims.text: steps_172044 : halts_in tm c0 (N.to_nat K) /\ forall n, halts_in tm c0 n -> n = N.to_nat K, with K = 853177647932005270554892218084645935472995035642746848454477793277027802995098762076895667304703808111420498351739937140047615589683 minus one: the machine reaches its halting configuration after exactly K steps and at no other time, so it runs for K + 1 steps with the halting transition (the bbchallenge count). Being exact, this is also the best possible lower and upper bound. Every lemma of the Coq proof states its number of steps (busycoq's multistep). A visit takes 6(n0+…+ni−1) + 4i + 11 steps. V visits take a closed form, 11V + 6V(V−1) plus a sum over the levels of the odometer (Jz), proved by induction on V. The run carries its count and ends with run 225 start = RHalt K.

claims.title: The machine halts from blank tape
claims.text: The simulator of lean/Sim.lean and lean/Run.lean, started on blank tape, meets the halting transition F0 within 108 rounds (about 88.9 million: 68.6 million single transitions, 13.4 million runs crossed, 86,734 jumps). With run_sound this is halts : HaltsFromBlank. The evaluation is compiled, so it trusts Lean's compiler; about 6 minutes of CPU.

claims.title: The visit rule of a zone, for every zone
claims.text: When the tape ends in counters (011)<sup>n<sub>k</sub></sup> … (011)<sup>n<sub>0</sub></sup> separated by 11 (bit 0) or 01 (bit 1), one visit is a binary increment of the bits: the lowest 0 bit s<sub>i</sub> is set, n<sub>i</sub> loses 1, every bit cleared moves one unit to the counter on its left, n<sub>0</sub> gains 2. Proved for every number of counters, every count and every tape left of the zone, by induction on the carry.

claims.title: V visits at once
claims.text: In the coordinates N<sub>0</sub> = n<sub>0</sub> − s<sub>1</sub>, N<sub>j</sub> = n<sub>j</sub> + s<sub>j</sub> − s<sub>j+1</sub> a visit is a plain binary increment in which N<sub>j−1</sub> loses 1 when bit j is set and N<sub>0</sub> gains 2. For every V after which the bits have not overflowed and every N<sub>j</sub> is still at least 2, the machine goes from the zone to the zone V visits later, given in closed form.

claims.title: The simulator follows the machine
claims.text: Each round of the run-length simulator (one transition, a run of a word crossed when one or two copies are crossed in the same state, a copy unpacked, or a jump whose hypotheses it has checked) takes the configuration it stands for to a configuration the machine reaches; if it answers true, the machine halts. The leftward half of the simulator is the mirror image of the rightward half (steps_mir).

claims.title: The number of steps, by three Python simulators
claims.text: 853177647932005270554892218084645935472995035642746848454477793277027802995098762076895667304703808111420498351739937140047615589683 steps (the halting transition counted), 9.6·1065 visits of the right end. The same number as the Coq proof; the Lean proof does not count steps. py/accel.py (86,729 closed-form jumps, 116,906 visits on a run-length tape), py/odo.py (the jumps composed by doubling instead of the closed form) and py/leansim.py (the Lean simulator's algorithm, 86,734 other jumps) give the same number.

claims.title: The Python simulators against a cell-by-cell run
claims.text: py/rl.py agrees with the cell-level reference simulator on step count and whole tape at each of the first 3,000 visits, with the plain C simulator on step count and number of 1s at each of the first 20,000 visits; the visit rule with its step count 6(n0+…+ni−1) + 4i + 11 agrees with the cell-level simulator on 6,000 random zones; the accelerated run agrees with rl.py alone up to visit 429,738 and with the C run-length simulator c/tok.c at 57 checkpoints up to step 1015.

claims.title: How it ends
claims.text: At the last visit the tape is 1 n214 01 n213 01 … 01 n0 0 with n214 = 91,562 and n0 about 2.5·1065: every bit is 1, the carry crosses all 215 counters in one walk of 2.9·1066 steps and F reads a 0 at the left end. The word at the left end had been eaten over the previous overflows (11111101111, 11111101, 11101111, 11101, 1111, 1).

claims.title: The irregular visits
claims.text: When a counter runs low or the bits overflow, the words between counters change (11101, 11101111, 1101101101, …) and counters merge or split; no closed rule is known for these visits, they are simulated (in the Lean proof too). The first counter ran out four times (near 105, 1014, 1039 and 1066 visits); three times the left end recovered, the fourth time it did not.

claims.title: Related holdouts
claims.text: The same table as 1RB0LC_1LC0RE_1LD1LB_1LA1LD_1RF0RA_---1RE up to renaming and mirroring, started in another state; no common configuration in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps of each.

explainer.title: This machine halts, after 8.5·10<sup>131</sup> steps
explainer.lede: Lean and Coq both prove that it halts, and Coq proves after exactly how many steps: a simulator that is proved to follow the machine runs it from blank tape to its halting transition. The machine keeps a binary odometer on its tape whose digits are fuel tanks; the tanks drain exponentially slowly, the odometer grows to 215 digits, and one day the carry runs off the left end of the tape. The simulator below runs the real machine, but it would need far longer than the age of the universe to get there.

facts.text: Proved in Coq, checked by the kernel; also in Lean.
Steps before it halts; the exact number is proved in Coq.
Cells of tape at the end, in 215 counters.
The odometer rule and its closed form for V visits, proved for all sizes.

sections.heading: From six states to an odometer of fuel tanks
html: The question "does this machine halt, and when?" can be asked at four levels of description. Each level keeps
less detail than the one above it and has a coarser unit of time, and each step down is a theorem saying that the
lower level follows the machine exactly. At the bottom a program built from levels 2 to 4 runs from blank tape to the
halting transition; that run is the proof (the bottom line).
A tape of cells and a head in one of six states. One unit of time is one step.
From blank tape to the halt: 8.53·10131 steps.
Level 2The compressed tape
The tape as runs of a short word, a run of a million copies being one item. One unit is one round: a transition, a whole run crossed, or one copy unpacked.
Kernel each round follows the machine: mstep_sound
Level 3Visits of a zone
The tape each time the head reaches new ground on the right, as counters of 011 with bits between them. One unit is one visit: 6(n0 + … + ni−1) + 4i + 11 steps.
Kernel a visit is a binary increment: visit
Level 4The odometer of tanks
The same counters in the coordinates Nj, where they are fuel tanks. One unit is one jump of V visits at once, up to 2214 of them.
Kernel V visits in closed form: jump
The visits that are not of the regular form (a tank nearly empty, or the binary number overflowing) have no rule
at level 3 or 4; the program runs them at level 2. Lean proves that whatever mixture of rounds and jumps the program
makes is a run of the machine (run_sound, kernel), and evaluates the program from blank tape with
compiled code (run_halts, native_decide). Coq does the same with the exact step count, checked by its

sections.heading: The compressed tape
html: The first step down replaces the tape by a compressed tape: two stacks of items, one on each side of the
head, where an item is a single cell or a word repeated n times, for any n. A round of the program
(mstep in lean/Sim.lean) is one of four things:
• a transition: the head reads the cell in front of it and the machine makes one step;
• a run crossed: in front of the head lies a run of copies of a word, and one copy, entered in some state,
is left on the far side in the same state. Then every copy is crossed in the same way, so the whole run is crossed
at once and the steps are multiplied out;
• two copies crossed: the same with two copies of the word taken together;
• a copy unpacked: otherwise one copy is taken off the run and written out as cells.
Leftward moves are handled by mirroring the table, so one rule covers both directions (steps_mir).
Kernel mstep_sound: every round leads from the configuration the stacks stand
for to the next one by real steps of the machine, whatever is on the stacks. How the program folds cells into runs
only affects its speed, never its correctness.
The stepper runs the program and the plain machine side by side. After every round the machine is moved on by the
number of steps the round claims, and the two tapes are compared cell by cell.

sections.heading: One visit is a binary increment
html: Look at the tape each time the head, in state A, steps onto a fresh cell at the right end (a visit). Write n for the word 011 repeated n times. Then the tape is a list of counters with two-cell words between them, for example at visit 59 (step 10,094):
The words between counters are 11 or 01. Read 11 as the bit 0 and 01 as the bit 1: the tape carries a binary number, one bit between each pair of counters.
<svg viewBox="0 0 600 170" role="img" aria-label="an odometer whose digits are fuel tanks" style="width:100%;max-width:600px;height:auto;font:12px var(--mono);">

<rect x="10" y="50" width="90" height="34" rx="5"/><rect x="140" y="50" width="90" height="34" rx="5"/><rect x="270" y="50" width="90" height="34" rx="5"/><rect x="400" y="50" width="120" height="34" rx="5"/></g>
<text x="120" y="42" fill="var(--muted)">bit 0</text><text x="250" y="42" fill="var(--muted)">bit 0</text><text x="380" y="42" fill="var(--muted)">bit 0</text>

<text x="55" y="104" fill="var(--muted)">−1 per 8</text><text x="185" y="104" fill="var(--muted)">−1 per 4</text><text x="315" y="104" fill="var(--muted)">−1 per 2</text><text x="460" y="104" fill="var(--muted)">+2 per visit</text>
<text x="300" y="140" fill="var(--fg2)">each visit adds 1 to the binary number written by the bits;</text>
<text x="300" y="158" fill="var(--fg2)">tank j pays one unit every 2^j visits</text></g></svg>

One visit adds 1 to that binary number, exactly as a car's odometer ticks: the bits at the right end that are 1 turn to 0, and the first 0 bit turns to 1. The head walks left only as far as that bit and comes back, so most visits are short.

The counters pay for it. The counter left of a bit loses one unit each time the bit is set (after the bookkeeping of the units that cleared bits pass along), and the last counter gains 2 at every visit. So the counter next to bit j is a tank that loses one unit every 2j visits: the last tanks drain fast, the first ones almost never. A visit that sets bit i takes 6(n0 + … + ni−1) + 4i + 11 steps.

Because the rule is this regular, any number of visits can be applied at once with a formula, as long as no tank runs low and the number does not overflow. That is what lets a program follow the machine for 10131 steps.
Kernel visit in lean/Zone.lean states this for every number of
counters, every count and every tape left of the zone: if inc, the increment with its bookkeeping,
applies to the bits and counts, the machine goes from the zone to the incremented zone. The proof follows the head:
it walks left through the counters behind the 1 bits (state D turns each 011 into 100),
turns at the 0 bit, and walks back (state C turns 100 into 011). inc gives no
answer when every bit is 1 (an overflow) or a count that must pay is 0; those visits are the irregular ones.
Type a zone (counts and the two-cell words between them, ending with n0 and the 0), choose what lies
left of it, and make a visit. The browser builds the tape, runs the real machine until the head is back in A at the
right end, and compares the result with the rule. The picture is the visit in space and time: one row per moment,

sections.heading: Many visits at once: the tanks
html: The bookkeeping of a visit (a count loses one, a cleared bit moves one unit up) looks fiddly in the counts
nj of the tape. In the coordinates
N_0 = n_0 − s_1,    N_j = n_j + s_j − s_(j+1),    N_k = n_k + s_k          (s_j the bits)
it becomes plain: at every visit N0 gains 2, and Nj−1 loses 1 each time bit j is set.
Bit j is set once every 2<sup>j</sup> visits, so N<sub>j−1</sub> is a fuel tank that drains at that rate, and after V
visits everything is known in closed form: bit j has seen about V/2<sup>j−1</sup> increments, half of which set it
Kernel jump: if the bits do not overflow within V visits and every
N<sub>j</sub> (j ≥ 1) is still at least 2 after them, the machine goes from the zone to the zone after V visits.
The proof is an induction on V: addV_succ says that one more increment after addV V is
addV (V + 1), and inc_physP that the increment in these coordinates is the visit rule of
the tape. The Coq proof adds the number of steps of V visits in closed form, a sum over the levels of the

sections.heading: Tanks that run dry, and overflows
html: When a tank is down to a few units, or when all bits are 1 and the carry runs past the last of them, the tidy picture breaks for a few visits: the words between counters become other short words (11101, 11101111, 1101101101, …), neighbouring counters merge or a new one splits off, and then an odometer is back with other contents. Nobody has a formula for these visits; the program runs them step by step on a compressed tape, where a run of a million copies of 011 is one item. There are 116,906 such visits in the whole run, between 86,729 formula jumps.
The first counter of the list is the slowest tank. It ran dry four times, near visits 105, 1014, 1039 and 1066. Three times the scrap it left at the left end turned back into a regular left end.

html: The fourth time, the scrap was a different word, 11101101111101111, and each later overflow of the whole odometer ate a piece of it: 11101101111101, 11101101101, 1101101, 11111101111, 11111101, 11101111, 11101, 1111, 1. With a single 1 left, the tape was

sections.heading: Proved in Coq and in Lean, step count included
html: The halt is a theorem checked by Lean. The proof has two parts. First, a small simulator written inside Lean is proved to follow the machine, whatever the tape: it keeps the tape compressed (a run of a million copies of 011 is one item), crosses a whole run when one copy is crossed in the same state, and at each visit may apply the odometer rule for many visits at once. That rule, and its formula for V visits, are proved for every odometer size. Second, Lean runs this simulator from blank tape: after about 89 million rounds it meets the halting transition. This last step is a compiled evaluation (native_decide), so it trusts Lean's compiler; everything else is checked by the kernel.

The same proof is also written in Coq, on the definitions of busycoq, the library in which the bbchallenge results are proved. There the run is evaluated by Coq's kernel virtual machine (vm_compute), so the Coq theorem does not trust a compiler. It is also faster, thanks to two more rules. When the odometer overflows, the head walks across every counter and back, and that walk is almost all of the work: 99% of the Lean simulator's rounds. A counter level looks like 1 0 (011)k 1 on the way left and (100)m 1 0 1 1 0 on the way back; the two rules cross such a level in one round, whatever k and m are, and are proved for every k and m. With them the run is 19 million rounds instead of 89 million, and takes under 3 minutes without counting steps.

The Lean proof shows that the machine halts, not after how many steps. The Coq proof also counts: every rule in it says exactly how many steps it takes, a visit of the odometer and a jump over many visits included, and the simulator adds them up as it runs. So the 132-digit number below is a theorem too, and being exact it is also the best possible lower and upper bound. It is the number the Python programs in the repository had computed: three simulators written separately, tested against a plain cell-by-cell simulator, give it as well. Counting makes the Coq run slower, about 8.5 minutes instead of under 3, because the formula for a jump multiplies numbers of a few hundred digits.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machine below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in the other, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.
